claims.text: The initial material is commercial-grade stainless steel, such as AISI 304 or AISI 316.
The untreated stainless-steel surface has a native passive oxide film.
Laser surface alloying can incorporate a Cr/Mo-rich powder into the stainless-steel surface.
Laser surface alloying with Cr and Mo produces a uniform alloyed surface layer.
The alloyed surface layer is enriched in chromium and molybdenum.
The laser-alloyed surface has a refined microstructure.
Chromium and molybdenum enrichment improves passivation of the stainless-steel surface.
Laser treatment rapidly melts and resolidifies the stainless-steel surface.
Rapid melting and resolidification enable the diffusion and incorporation of chromium and molybdenum into the surface.
Incorporated chromium and molybdenum promote formation of a more stable and protective passive oxide layer.
The modified passive layer slows metal dissolution.
The modified passive layer suppresses pitting corrosion by increasing the local concentration of corrosion-inhibiting elements.
Laser-alloyed stainless steel will have a lower corrosion current density than untreated stainless steel under identical conditions.
Laser-alloyed stainless steel will have a higher pitting potential than untreated stainless steel under identical conditions.
Lower corrosion current density and higher pitting potential indicate improved corrosion resistance.
The corrosion-resistance enhancement depends on laser power, scan speed, and powder-delivery parameters.
Severe mechanical stress or thermal cycling may reduce the corrosion-resistance enhancement.
